description: Hi, I’m Vincent from Taiwan. My background is in computer science, machine learning, and Python. I’m forming a team to build a wildfire activity dashboard using NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite data. We’ll test whether a simple ML model can make hotspot counts from the two sensors more comparable. I’d love to team up with people interested in geospatial data, web development, data visualization, or science communication.
summary:
Fire Signal Agreement is an interactive dashboard that helps users compare satellite fire observations without mistaking differences between sensors for changes in fire activity. Using NASA FIRMS Terra/Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS hotspot data, we developed a weekly burning calendar, machine-learning calibration models, and an evidence-grounded AI assistant for a western U.S. study region.

Our system translates MODIS detection counts onto a shared VIIRS reference scale while keeping original observations available for comparison. Models trained on 2023–2024 data were evaluated on held-out 2025 observations. XGBoost reduced mean absolute error by approximately 51% compared with linear regression. Users can explore the calendar, inspect discrepancies, and ask supported questions answered from verified tables and curated NASA documentation.

The project addresses the challenge by making Earth-observation records easier to compare and interpret transparently. This matters because satellite hotspot detections are not counts of individual fires: sensor characteristics can affect apparent patterns. By showing calibration results, source evidence, and limitations together, Fire Signal Agreement supports more informed analysis of fire activity.
details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

We built Fire Signal Agreement to explore a simple question: when two satellites report different numbers of hotspots, how should we interpret the difference?

The dashboard uses NASA FIRMS fire-detection data from Terra/Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS for a western U.S. region covering 37–42°N and 125–119°W. It organizes the observations into weekly counts for 2023–2025 and displays them in an interactive burning calendar.

To make the records easier to compare, we trained linear regression and XGBoost models to estimate VIIRS-equivalent hotspot counts from MODIS observations. We trained on 2023–2024 and evaluated the models separately on 2025. XGBoost achieved a mean absolute error of 80.81 detections per week, compared with 163.96 for linear regression—about a 51% improvement.

Users can switch between calibrated estimates and observed VIIRS counts, inspect the original records, and download the results. A local AI assistant answers supported questions about weekly counts, model performance, and sensor differences. Numerical answers come from database calculations, while explanations use curated NASA documentation with source links.

2. What benefits does it have?

The dashboard brings observations, model results, and explanations into one place. Users can spot an unusual week, inspect the numbers behind it, and investigate why the sensors might disagree.

Keeping the original observations visible also lets users judge the calibration results themselves. They can see where a model performs well and where large differences remain.

3. What is the intended impact?

We hope to help students, researchers, and other users interpret satellite fire records more carefully. Differences in detection counts can reflect sensor characteristics as well as changes in fire activity.

Our project gives users a practical way to explore those differences while keeping the evidence and limitations visible. It is a regional research prototype, and its performance outside the study area has not been established.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did you use?

We used Python for data processing and application development, with pandas, scikit-learn, and XGBoost for analysis and modeling. SQLite stores the processed data, while Streamlit and Altair power the dashboard and charts.

The local assistant uses Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct through vLLM on an NVIDIA RTX 3090. Docker Compose runs the dashboard and model server together.

We checked the implementation with 102 automated tests, reconciliation against the original archives, and a small live assistant benchmark.

5. How is your project creative?

Our approach connects a visual calendar, sensor-calibration models, and an evidence-grounded assistant in one workflow.

For example, a user can notice a large difference in the calendar, examine that week’s observations and prediction error, and ask the assistant about the result. The assistant retrieves verified information, and Python calculates the numerical answer. This makes the interaction useful while keeping its supporting evidence accessible.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We paid particular attention to the meaning and limitations of the data. Hotspots are satellite pixel detections, not counts of individual fires. Sensor resolution, observation timing, and detection characteristics can affect the recorded counts.

We also kept 2025 separate from training so we could evaluate the models on unseen observations. Calibrated estimates remain separate from measured counts, and the dashboard labels training-period fits and held-out results clearly.

For readability, we used consistent color scales across years and contrast-aware calendar labels. For reproducibility, exported results include source and model metadata.

Finally, we made uncertainty explicit: a week with no records does not prove there was no fire, and our calibration does not correct for unknown observing coverage. We wanted users to understand both what the prototype shows and where further investigation is needed.
